$comment: THE FIELD GUIDE. One entry per kind of file met in the wild: the signals that identify it, what it is FOR in a university, how it is handled, and what has already gone wrong with it. `scripts/identify.mjs` evaluates `when` against the facts it measures, so this file is data and not prose; `docs/FIELD-GUIDE.md` is generated from it and must never be edited by hand. Every `seen` field names a real file. Add an entry the day a new shape turns up, with the document that showed it.

census.note: 2,325 files under the course back catalogue and one operator's downloads. Every count in an entry comes from that census or from running the intake chain over it.

facts.$comment: What identify.mjs measures on each file. An entry's `when` keys one of these; a value is either a literal to equal or a comparison string (">0", "0", ">=40", "<10").
facts.ext: the extension, lowercased, with the dot
facts.kind: what the FIRST BYTES say it is: zip, pdf, ole, jpeg, png, gif, rtf, ps, text, unknown
facts.extMatchesBytes: true when the extension agrees with the bytes
facts.ooxml: for a zip: word, excel, powerpoint, or other-zip
facts.generator: docProps/app.xml <Application>, empty when the writer did not set one
facts.headingStyles: paragraph styles resolving to a heading level, through outlineLvl and basedOn
facts.oMath: count of <m:oMath>, which is the only place Word keeps an equation
facts.literalBullets: bullet characters typed into the text rather than applied as numbering
facts.wdp: HD Photo sidecar files inside the archive
facts.currency: currency signs in the body text
facts.excelFormulas: spreadsheet function calls written into the text
facts.htmlPasteStyles: style ids that only exist because HTML was pasted in (MsoNormal, KaTeX class names)
facts.semanticStyles: paragraph styles the AUTHOR created, by Word's own w:customStyle flag, that are not headings; their names are what the author said each paragraph is for
facts.accentStrippedStyles: style ids that are a non-English word with its accents removed, which is what Word does to a localised style name
facts.textLayer: for a pdf: true when it carries extractable text
facts.pdfProducer: the /Producer string, which says what made the PDF
facts.wordsPerEquation: words divided by equations, which is how dense a document's maths is; null when it has none
facts.pdfPages: for a pdf: how many pages it draws
facts.imageWhole: for a jpeg, png or gif: true when the file ends in its own end marker (JPEG EOI, PNG IEND, GIF trailer); false is a file cut off part-way

entries.name: Word, written in Word
entries.purpose: The ordinary summary. Somebody wrote it in Word and used the heading styles, so the document carries its own structure.
entries.handling: open-docx.js, then docx.js. The heading level is read from the style's outlineLvl, which is Word's own answer and does not depend on what the style is called.
entries.seen: 215 of 248 Word documents name Microsoft Office Word as their generator. SUMMARY_Introduction_to_Math: 1,615 paragraphs, 146 headings, 1,249 equations.
entries.gotcha: The generator is what makes this claim honest. Word ALWAYS writes <Application> into docProps/app.xml, so a document with headings and no generator was written somewhere else and belongs to google-docs-export instead.

entries.name: Word whose styles are named in another language
entries.purpose: The author's Word is not in English, so its built-in styles are not either. Nothing about the content is unusual, and the author has no idea anything is different.
entries.handling: Nothing special, because the level never comes from the name. A style carries outlineLvl in its own definition or inherits it through basedOn, and that is what makes it a heading.
entries.seen: Draft Summary.docx: heading styles Cmsor1 to Cmsor7, which is Word writing the Hungarian Cimsor with the accents stripped out of the id. Accounting_Formula_Sheet: Egyenlet (equation) and Stlus3, Stlus4 (style).
entries.gotcha: A rule that looks for a style called Heading finds nothing here and concludes the document is unstructured. The old extractor found 0 headings in Draft Summary; reading outlineLvl finds 18.

entries.name: Word carrying real equations
entries.purpose: Any quantitative course. The equations are OOXML maths objects, not text, so they are invisible to anything that reads runs.
entries.handling: omml.js, reached through docx.js, then katex-check.js before a manifest exists.
entries.seen: 87 of 248 Word documents. 15,546 equations across the 134 summaries; one document holds 1,249.
entries.gotcha: mammoth and python-docx drop <m:oMath> in SILENCE. The document comes out looking clean and missing every formula. This is the most expensive failure in the whole intake, because nothing about the result looks wrong.

entries.name: Word with a web page pasted into it
entries.purpose: An author copied from a rendered page (a wiki, a lecture site, a maths page) straight into Word. The paste brings the page's CSS classes with it as Word styles.
entries.handling: Converts normally. The tell is a styles.xml full of names no author chose.
entries.seen: Four accounting summaries carry KaTeX's own class names as Word styles: katex, base, strut, mord, msupsub, vlist, alongside msonormal0 from an HTML paste.
entries.gotcha: Maths that was pasted as RENDERED HTML is not an equation any more; it is styled text that looks right and carries no <m:oMath>. Check the equation count against what the document appears to contain: these four had OMML as well, so the paste was not the whole document, but a document where oMath is 0 and the pages are full of formulas has lost every one of them.

entries.name: Word written on the house template
entries.purpose: The summary template gives the author named styles for the things a summary is made of, so the author has already said which paragraph is an example, which is a recap, and which is not their prose at all.
entries.handling: Convert normally. `docx.js` writes each one into the Markdown as `<!-- style: In Short -->` above its paragraph, and the layout phase reads those instead of guessing. What a name may BECOME on the page is the platform's vocabulary: ask content_guide, never a list kept here.
entries.seen: SUMMARY_Micro carries 37 marked paragraphs: Example (18), In Short (18) and not-prose (1). CHEAT_SHEET_Applied_Statistics adds Summary. GG_SummaryTemplate2026.dotx is the template itself.
entries.gotcha: This is the one piece of authorial intent in the whole file and every extractor that asked only whether a style is a heading threw it away. Word marks these itself with w:customStyle="1", so finding them needs no list of names to keep up to date.

entries.name: A Word template, not a document
entries.purpose: The house format itself: the styles every summary is written on. It is what a new summary starts from, and it is not course content.
entries.handling: Never a source. Read it to learn what the house styles MEAN, which is what makes word-semantic-template readable.
entries.seen: GG_SummaryTemplate2026.dotx, GG_Template2025.docx
entries.gotcha: It parses perfectly and produces a document of placeholder text. Nothing about the output says it was a template.

entries.name: Word with no styles at all
entries.purpose: Usually a Google Docs export, sometimes a document somebody typed without ever touching the style menu. Either way the heading level exists only as a font size.
entries.handling: docx2.js, NOT docx.js, and then LOOK at the result. It ranks the distinct font sizes above the body size into levels, which is typography and not structure.
entries.seen: 35 of 248 Word documents carry no pStyle. Most are short notes; the substantial ones are Questions tutorial C (178 paragraphs), RoughTimeLine (165) and Assg1 draft (104).
entries.gotcha: docx.js does not fail on these; it used to flatten the document to one level in silence, and nothing downstream could tell that from a document that genuinely has no headings. It now exits non-zero and says so.

entries.name: Word, exported from Google Docs
entries.purpose: The author wrote it in Google Docs and downloaded it as Word. Common, because Docs is what a laptop already has.
entries.handling: Whether docx.js works depends on the document: Docs writes real heading styles when the author used its own heading menu, and nothing when they only made the text bigger. Run docx.js and believe what it reports.
entries.seen: 33 of 248 Word documents set no <Application> in docProps/app.xml, which Word always sets. Nevtelen dokumentum.docx is a Docs document that was never even named.
entries.gotcha: An absent generator is a better signal than a missing style: Word ALWAYS writes one, so its absence means the file came from somewhere else, whatever the rest of it looks like.

entries.name: Word that is still being reviewed
entries.purpose: A draft somebody has commented on. The comments are a conversation about the text, not part of it.
entries.handling: Converts normally and the comments do not come with it, because they live in a separate part. Treat the document as a DRAFT: somebody is still arguing with it.
entries.seen: 24 of 248 Word documents carry word/comments.xml, including all seven Week N.docx files of one course.
entries.gotcha: Nothing in the extracted text says the document was still being argued over, so a course can be built from a draft nobody signed off.

entries.name: Word with tracked changes still in it
entries.purpose: A document mid-edit, where the file holds both what it said and what it will say.
entries.handling: NOT HANDLED. The extractor reads every run, so deleted text comes through as if it were still there and the result is a mix of two drafts. Accept the changes in Word first.
entries.seen: None yet, in 248 Word documents. Listed because the failure is silent and the fix is somebody else's ten seconds.
entries.gotcha: Text inside <w:del> reads exactly like text that was never deleted.

entries.name: Word with pictures, text boxes and drawn shapes
entries.purpose: An author pasted a graph into a heading, or floated a label over the text. Ordinary authoring, and invisible in the text stream.
entries.handling: One ordered pass over the document, never a walk over paragraph-shaped chunks.
entries.seen: 30 of 248 documents carry text boxes and 40 carry VML shapes. SUMMARY_Introduction_to_Math: 53 pictures, 10 text boxes, 16 shapes.
entries.gotcha: A paragraph-based scan found 32 of those 53 pictures, 0 of the 10 text boxes and 3 of the 16 shapes. A text box and a drawn shape are the two defects no text diff can see.

entries.name: Word's HD Photo sidecars
entries.purpose: None for us. Word writes an alternate-format copy beside each real picture.
entries.handling: Excluded from the media inventory. They are never content.
entries.seen: 35 of 248 documents. 45 of the 98 media files in SUMMARY_Introduction_to_Math.
entries.gotcha: Counting them reported 66 unreferenced images and buried the 2 that were genuinely orphaned.

entries.name: A cheat sheet
entries.purpose: A one-page formula reference a student revises from. Almost all symbols, almost no prose, and one of the most useful things a course holds.
entries.handling: Converts normally. Its shape means the usual assumptions do not hold: it is not a lecture, it has no sections worth the name, and its density is the point.
entries.seen: 10 of 248 documents. CHEAT_SHEET Applied Statistics: 530 words carrying 89 equations.
entries.gotcha: A word-count rule that decides a document is too thin rejects exactly these, and a no-headings rule flags them as broken when they are simply a list. The length is part of the identity: a 12,000-word summary with dense maths is a maths course, not a cheat sheet, and only the word count separates the two.

entries.name: Word where the equations are spreadsheet formulas
entries.purpose: A data or analytics course teaching Excel. The author typed the formulas into Word's equation editor because that is where formulas go.
entries.handling: Converts, but these are not mathematics and should not become formula blocks. They are code, and a code span reads better than a refused equation.
entries.seen: 4 of 248 documents. Introduction to Data Analytics: SUMIF, SUMIFS, ROUND, IF among 100 equations.
entries.gotcha: An underscore inside a function name is a LaTeX escape problem and a dollar in a cell reference is a delimiter problem. Both refused equations before they were fixed.

entries.name: A summary about money
entries.purpose: Accounting, finance, operations. Prose full of amounts, and amounts inside the equations too.
entries.handling: Converts normally. The currency in prose is prose; the currency inside an equation is written as an escaped dollar.
entries.seen: 99 of 248 documents. Operations and Supply Chain, Accounting, Intermediate Accounting.
entries.gotcha: This one shape caused five separate bugs. A dollar in prose pairs with the next one and everything between becomes an equation: on one summary that made a single 5,000-character span covering half a chapter. Pandoc's delimiter rule settles it, but only if an ESCAPED dollar is not allowed to close a span, which is the mistake that turned 5 refusals across the corpus into 24 in one run.

entries.name: An accounting summary, which is mostly tables
entries.purpose: Journal entries, ledgers and trial balances are tables, and a summary of them is a document made of tables with prose between.
entries.handling: Converts to GitHub-flavoured Markdown tables. A journal entry is Account / Debit / Credit and stays that way; the layout phase has element types for these and must not invent its own.
entries.seen: 147 of 248 documents carry tables at all. Summary_Intermediate_Accounting: 154 tables. SUMMARY_Accounting: 91.
entries.gotcha: A cell holds ONE line: a newline in it ends the table, and an unescaped pipe opens a column that is not there. Merged cells make rows of different widths, and a separator row narrower than the header silently drops every column past it.

entries.name: PDF with a real text layer
entries.purpose: Course manuals, past exams, answer keys, grading schemes, tutorial sheets. Almost everything a university publishes that is not the summary itself.
entries.handling: Readable, and refused as a SOURCE for a summary. It is an input to Analyze and a checklist item, not something to convert into a lesson.
entries.seen: 1,131 PDFs in the census. 24 past exams and answer keys, two course manuals, eight tutorial sheets, four grading schemes.
entries.gotcha: The PDF extractor needs four hand-tuned parameters per document (font map, page list, size map, footer pattern) and none can be guessed. It is not a general reader and must never be offered as one.

entries.name: A PDF a lecturer made in LaTeX
entries.purpose: Problem sets, lecture notes and exams from a mathematics or economics department. The most carefully typeset thing in the course and the hardest to read back.
entries.handling: Text extraction works, and the maths does not: LaTeX-made PDFs draw formulas as positioned glyphs, so an integral comes out as scattered letters. Retype the formulas from the rendered page; never trust the extracted text for them.
entries.seen: 36 PDFs from pdfTeX, plus 7 from dvips and Ghostscript together.
entries.gotcha: The prose extracts beautifully, which makes it look as though the whole document did.

entries.name: A PDF somebody printed from Word
entries.purpose: The summary, exported. It is the same document as the .docx, one generation later and with everything structural removed.
entries.handling: Refused as a source. GO AND FIND THE .docx: it exists, somebody made this from it, and it carries the headings, the numbering and the equations that this does not.
entries.seen: 125 PDFs name a Microsoft product as their producer, and 7 more say Microsoft: Print To PDF. Almost every summary in the catalogue sits beside its own PDF twin.
entries.gotcha: It is the most tempting wrong answer in the whole intake, because it looks complete and it opens.

entries.name: A scan with no text layer
entries.purpose: A photographed or scanned handout, an old exam paper, a whiteboard. Common for anything predating the course's own digital records.
entries.handling: NOT HANDLED. There is no OCR in this pipeline. Say so plainly, record it as a missing input, and ask for a digital original.
entries.seen: 455 PDFs carry no /Producer at all, which is where these live. None has yet been needed as a source.
entries.gotcha: An empty extract from a scan looks exactly like an empty extract from a broken parse. Detect the absent text layer and say which it is.

entries.name: A PDF wearing a .docx extension
entries.purpose: Usually a summary somebody exported to PDF and renamed, hoping it would be accepted.
entries.handling: Refused at preflight on the magic bytes. Go and find the Word file it came from.
entries.seen: SUMMARY_IHC_(GradeGuru).docx, in four places in the catalogue. Social_Psychology_Lectures_EN.docx.
entries.gotcha: Two of four files on one real upload were this. It is common enough to check every time.

entries.name: A Word file wearing a .pdf extension
entries.purpose: Somebody renamed it, or a download went wrong. This one is GOOD NEWS: the file is better than its name.
entries.handling: Rename it and convert it normally. Do not discard it as a PDF, which is what a rule keyed on the extension does.
entries.seen: 10 files. Among them 2019-20 Exam.pdf and 2023-24 Exam.pdf, sitting in a live course workspace as past exams, and SUMMARY(Preview)_IHC_(GradeGuru).pdf.
entries.gotcha: The pipeline refuses PDF as a source, so the extension alone decided these were unusable. They are Word documents.

entries.name: A photograph wearing a .docx extension
entries.purpose: None. A file was renamed, or a download went wrong. It is not the document anybody meant to send.
entries.handling: Refused at preflight on the magic bytes. Go and find the real file; there is nothing to salvage.
entries.seen: IBA1_IB_Literature_Summary.docx, 32 KB, JPEG magic.
entries.gotcha: The extension is not evidence, and neither is the size: 32 KB is a plausible size for a short document.

entries.name: A note somebody left instead of the file
entries.purpose: A person told you something and the filesystem swallowed it. The file is a sentence.
entries.handling: Read it. It is an answer to a question about the course, not an input.
entries.seen: 2020-21 Exam.pdf, in a live course workspace, whose entire contents are: Not gonna do a summary for this.
entries.gotcha: It is named like a past exam and sits in a folder of past exams. Nothing but opening it says otherwise.

entries.name: Lecture slides
entries.purpose: What the lecturer actually showed. Often the only statement of what is examinable, and the thing students ask about most.
entries.handling: NOT HANDLED. There is no PowerPoint reader here. Slides are an input to Analyze, read by a person, and never a source of record.
entries.seen: 68 .pptx files in the census.
entries.gotcha: A deck is not prose and would not become one: its structure is one idea per slide with the argument in the speaker's mouth. Converting it would produce something that reads like a summary and is not one.

entries.name: A spreadsheet
entries.purpose: Grade books, datasets a statistics course works on, financial models an accounting course builds.
entries.handling: NOT HANDLED as a source. A dataset a course teaches ON belongs in materials, not in a lesson.
entries.seen: 104 .xlsx files in the census.
entries.gotcha: A summary that teaches a spreadsheet writes its formulas as text; see spreadsheet-formulas-as-equations. The spreadsheet itself is a different thing.

entries.name: The old binary Word format
entries.purpose: Anything written before 2007, or by somebody who never changed the default. Still turns up from university archives.
entries.handling: NOT HANDLED. It is a compound OLE file and shares nothing with a .docx. Open it in Word and save as .docx; that conversion is lossless and takes a moment.
entries.seen: None in this census, which is itself worth knowing: .doc has finally gone.
entries.gotcha: It is not a zip, so every tool here fails on it at the first byte, which is at least honest.

entries.name: An image that is not the format it claims
entries.purpose: A screenshot. A phone or an operating system saved PNG bytes under a .jpg name, or something re-encoded it on the way.
entries.handling: Harmless for a figure, because the bytes are read and not the name. It matters when a tool picks an encoder by extension.
entries.seen: 17 files, all named IMG_NNNN.jpg and all PNG.
entries.gotcha: Listed because the same mistake at document scale is the expensive one, and because it proves the rename happens by accident and not by intent.

entries.name: A picture cut off part-way
entries.purpose: A figure whose bytes stop before the file's own end marker. It keeps its header, so it sniffs as its format, reports a size and opens in most viewers, with a grey bottom half where the missing rows were.
entries.handling: Never upload it and never let a model 'repair' it: go back to the source (the Word document's word/media, the deck, the export) and take the bytes again. images.mjs refuses one before it leaves the machine, naming the file; the platform's door decodes every upload and refuses one that is not whole with 'not a whole file'. A file garbled in the middle that still ends correctly passes this check and not the door's, so look at the contact sheet before pushing.
entries.seen: Production storage, 16-18 September 2026: pictures emitted as base64 by a model whose output was cut off, then retried smaller until one fit. Personality Psychology keys 065633aae1d5 (5,307 B), cd9dcb3582aa (1,104 B), 3d6b0ffbdb38 and b9fd3464a883 (467 B each) stop before EOI; 65 pictures across two courses had to be restored.
entries.gotcha: Every cheap check is fooled: the header is intact, the size decodes, a ContentImage row is written, and the page draws something. Only reading to the end of the file, or decoding all of it, tells a cut-off picture from a whole one.

entries.name: An iPhone photograph
entries.purpose: A student photographed a whiteboard, a worked solution, or a page of a book.
entries.handling: NOT HANDLED. Nothing in this pipeline reads HEIC, and the reader will not serve it. Convert to PNG or JPEG first; macOS Preview does it.
entries.seen: 7 files.
entries.gotcha: It previews fine on a Mac, so it looks like a working image right up to the upload.

entries.name: A saved web page
entries.purpose: Somebody archived a page from the university's learning environment, usually because it was about to disappear.
entries.handling: NOT HANDLED. Read it in a browser and decide what it is; there is nothing here that parses one.
entries.seen: 15 files, alongside 34 plain .html.
entries.gotcha: It is one file containing an entire page and its assets, so its size says nothing about how much content it holds.
